From FASTQ to Nextflow
You can understand modern bioinformatics workflow engineering without already being a programmer. This book starts with ordinary sequencing files and shell commands, then develops one small analysis into a reproducible Nextflow workflow that can run locally or through an HPC scheduler.

Who this book is for
This book is written for biologists who can use a web browser but may not yet know what a shell, software channel, container image, workflow channel or job scheduler is. Every new term is introduced before it is relied upon.






ImportantScientific scope



The example uses deterministic synthetic paired-end reads derived from human GRCh38 chromosome 22. It contains no patient data. It is a teaching and reproducibility artifact—not a clinical pipeline, a WGBS pipeline or a production-scale biological analysis.

title: Preface
text:
Companion project
This tutorial grew from a real workflow-portability exercise on the DLDCC HPC cluster at Baylor College of Medicine. The useful parts were not only the successful commands. The difficult parts—an incompatible Java garbage collector, a full home-directory quota, a broken package solve, container PATH differences and non-identical BAM headers—exposed the engineering ideas that a beginner most needs to understand.
The book therefore preserves failures as teaching material. An error message is not evidence that you are unsuited to computational work. It is an observation about a system. The goal is to learn how to turn that observation into a small, testable hypothesis.
The commands and evidence are grounded in version v0.1.0 of the NGS Workflow Portability Lab. Linking the book to a tagged release prevents the underlying example from silently changing while someone is following the tutorial.

title: 1  The whole shebang
text:
1.1 Why a biologist should care
Imagine that you receive paired-end sequencing reads and answer a biological question with four programs. You record the commands in a notebook. Six months later, one program has changed, a library is missing and the commands run in the wrong order on a new computer. A collaborator cannot reproduce the result. On an HPC cluster, the same commands compete for memory or accidentally run on the login node.
The biological logic may have been correct. The engineering around it was not strong enough to preserve and communicate that logic.
Modern bioinformatics therefore has two inseparable responsibilities:
This book concentrates on the second responsibility without pretending it can replace the first. A beautifully engineered workflow can still run an inappropriate aligner. A biologically appropriate analysis can still be unreproducible if its software and execution are undocumented. Industry teams need both kinds of judgment.

1.2 Engineering objective
Before installing or coding anything, we need a map of the system. You should be able to point to each layer and answer:

What problem does this layer solve?
What information enters and leaves it?
Which other layer does it depend on?
What evidence tells us that it behaved as intended?

If these layers are blurred together, troubleshooting becomes guesswork. For example, changing a Conda package cannot fix a SLURM account error, and changing a Nextflow channel cannot repair a corrupt FASTQ file.

text:
1.3 Start with files and transformations
Most command-line bioinformatics programs behave like transformations:
input files + parameters + software → output files + logs
In our teaching project:

FastQC reads FASTQ files and writes quality reports.
Trim Galore reads paired FASTQ files and writes trimmed paired FASTQ files plus reports.
Bowtie2 reads trimmed FASTQ files and a reference index, then writes SAM alignment records.
SAMtools sorts, indexes and validates the alignments in BAM format.

Each program is a tool. A tool normally performs one focused operation. Connecting the tools creates a pipeline.





flowchart LR
    R["Paired FASTQ"] --> Q1["Raw FastQC"]
    R --> T["Trim Galore"]
    T --> Q2["Post-trim FastQC"]
    T --> A["Bowtie2"]
    X["Reference index"] --> A
    A --> S["SAMtools sort"]
    S --> V["BAM validation"]


 The analytical path used throughout the book. Trimming creates two branches: post-trim quality control and alignment. 



Notice that this is not simply a list. Raw FastQC and trimming can begin from the same input. Post-trim FastQC and alignment must wait for trimming. Alignment also needs the reference index. These dependencies form a directed graph.

text:
1.4 Tool, command, script, pipeline and workflow
These words are related but not interchangeable.








Term
Meaning in this book
Example




Tool
A program that performs a focused operation
samtools


Command
One request to run a program with particular arguments
samtools quickcheck sample.bam


Script
A saved text file containing commands and control logic
run_manual.sh


Pipeline
The connected analytical steps from input to result
FASTQ → trim → align → BAM


Workflow
An executable model of tasks, dependencies, inputs, outputs and resources
main.nf


Workflow run
One execution of a workflow with specific inputs, settings and software
the five-task chr22 run



A Bash script can implement a pipeline. A workflow engine adds explicit task contracts, dependency scheduling, isolated work directories, caching, resource requests and alternative execution backends. That does not make Bash obsolete: every Nextflow process in this book ultimately runs shell commands.

1.5 The complete stack
Our analytical graph sits inside a larger engineering system.





flowchart TB
    BQ["Biological question"] --> DATA["Input data + metadata"]
    DATA --> WF["Nextflow workflow logic"]
    SW["Software layer<br/>Conda environment or OCI image"] --> WF
    CFG["Parameters + configuration"] --> WF
    WF --> EX["Executor<br/>local or SLURM"]
    EX --> RT["Task runtime<br/>host, Conda or Singularity"]
    RT --> OUT["Outputs + logs + reports"]
    OUT --> QC["Technical and biological review"]
    GIT["Git + GitHub<br/>history and collaboration"] -. records .-> WF
    GIT -. records .-> CFG
    CI["CI/CD automation"] -. checks and publishes .-> GIT


 The layers are complementary. Nextflow coordinates commands supplied by an environment or image and launches tasks through an executor. 



The arrows do not mean that Git executes FastQC or that SLURM installs SAMtools. Each layer has a narrower responsibility.

1.6 The host operating system
The host is the computer or compute node on which a process ultimately runs. It supplies the kernel, processors, memory, filesystems and security controls. On a laptop you may administer much of the host. On an institutional cluster, platform administrators control it.
This matters because neither Conda nor a container creates CPUs or memory. Containers also share the host kernel; they are not complete virtual machines. Architecture and operating-system compatibility still matter.
Question answered by the host: What machine resources and operating-system services exist?

1.7 Cluster modules
An HPC module system lets administrators offer multiple versions of cluster-provided software. Loading a module commonly modifies environment variables such as PATH, which controls where the shell searches for executables.
Examples might include Java, Singularity or a compiler. Module names and versions are local to the cluster.
Question answered by modules: Which administrator-provided software should this shell session see?
Modules are not Conda environments. A module may expose the Java needed to start Nextflow while a Conda environment supplies FastQC and SAMtools. Because both can modify PATH, they can also conflict. Later we will inspect the active layers rather than assuming which executable is being used.

1.8 Conda environments and channels
Conda is a package and environment manager. A Conda environment is an isolated directory containing selected programs and their dependencies. For example, SAMtools depends on libraries for compressed genomic file formats. Conda attempts to choose a compatible set.
A channel is a package repository. It is a source from which Conda obtains package metadata and package files. Bioconda distributes many bioinformatics packages; conda-forge distributes a broad range of supporting software and libraries. Channel order and priority affect which builds the solver may select.
Question answered by Conda: Which package versions and compatible libraries are installed in this environment?
Conda improves control over software, but an environment specification alone does not freeze the host kernel, scheduler, external reference data or every future package build. Reproducibility has multiple layers.

1.9 OCI images, Docker and containers
An OCI image is a packaged, read-only filesystem plus metadata describing how software should run. OCI refers to open container standards. Docker is one widely used platform for building and running OCI-compatible images.
A container is a running process created from an image. The distinction is similar to a class recipe versus one instantiated object, or a cake recipe versus one baked cake—although every analogy has limits.
An image can contain the Conda-resolved tools, their libraries and selected operating-system files. A registry such as GitHub Container Registry stores and distributes images.








Concept
Mutable while building/running?
Role




Dockerfile
Yes, it is source text
Recipe for building an image


Image
Normally treated as immutable
Packaged filesystem and metadata


Tag
Can be moved to another image
Human-friendly name such as v0.1.0


Digest
Identifies exact image content
Immutable content address


Container
Has a writable runtime layer
A process running from an image


Registry
Stores and distributes images
GHCR, Docker Hub or another service



Question answered by an image: What packaged userspace and tools should travel with this task?






WarningA tag is not an immutable identity



The label latest can point to different image content tomorrow. A digest identifies exact content. Friendly tags are useful for humans; digests are stronger evidence for an exact runtime.

text:
1.10 Singularity and Apptainer on HPC
Docker normally relies on a long-running privileged service called a daemon. Multi-user HPC centers commonly do not allow users to run that service. They often provide Singularity or Apptainer, which can execute container images using an HPC-oriented security and filesystem model.
Singularity can pull an OCI image and create a SIF—a Singularity Image Format file. Nextflow can then execute individual tasks inside that SIF while SLURM assigns the compute node.
Docker and Singularity therefore are not two words for the same operation in our project:

GitHub Actions uses a Docker-oriented build process to create the OCI image.
DLDCC uses Singularity to run the resulting image as a SIF.

Question answered by Singularity: How should this HPC task enter and run the packaged container environment?

1.12 Executors and SLURM
An executor is the Nextflow component that decides how tasks are launched. With the local executor, tasks run on the current machine. With the SLURM executor, Nextflow writes job wrappers and submits them to the cluster scheduler.
SLURM is a workload manager. It places jobs on shared compute resources according to requested CPUs, memory, time, partition, account and site policy. It tracks queued, running, completed and failed jobs.
SLURM does not understand that trimming must precede alignment. Nextflow knows the data dependency and submits the alignment task only when its inputs exist. Nextflow does not decide which physical node is free. SLURM does.
Question answered by the executor and scheduler: How, where and when should this ready task run?

text:
1.14 CI/CD: automated feedback and delivery
Continuous integration (CI) means automatically integrating and checking small changes frequently. A CI workflow may lint files, render documentation, run a small test and verify that a container contains required tools.
Continuous delivery means keeping a tested artifact ready to release or publishing it through a controlled process. Continuous deployment goes further: a passing change is automatically deployed to its target environment.
In our work:

GitHub Actions building and smoke-checking an image is CI plus artifact delivery.
GitHub Actions publishing this Quarto book to GitHub Pages is automated deployment of documentation.
Running a research pipeline on new samples is not automatically “CI/CD.” It is a workflow execution and may require separate authorization, review and data controls.

Automation supplies evidence; it does not create scientific truth. A green check means the configured checks passed—not that every biological or clinical requirement has been validated.
Question answered by CI/CD: Which checks and publication actions should happen automatically when source changes or a release is created?

text:
1.15 Trace one sample through the stack
Consider the sample identifier sim_chr22.

Two FASTQ files and sample metadata describe the input.
Git identifies the exact workflow, configuration, environment and container recipe revision.
Nextflow creates the raw-QC and trimming tasks because both can consume the original read pair.
The selected profile tells Nextflow to use the local or SLURM executor and a Conda environment or Singularity image.
On DLDCC, Nextflow submits a job wrapper to SLURM.
SLURM assigns a compute node with the requested resources.
Singularity starts the task inside the project SIF and makes required host paths visible through bind mounts.
FastQC or Trim Galore runs with the inputs staged by Nextflow.
The task writes output and logs in its isolated work directory.
Nextflow records task status, publishes selected results and enables cache reuse.
Technical checks confirm that files exist, are readable and have expected summaries.
A qualified analyst still decides whether the results are biologically meaningful for the intended use.

No single technology performs all twelve responsibilities.

text:
1.16 Three kinds of reproducibility
The word reproducible is often used too broadly. In this book we separate:

Computational repeatability: rerunning the same inputs, code, parameters and runtime produces acceptably equivalent outputs.
Computational reproducibility: another person can reconstruct the analysis from recorded source, software, data provenance and instructions.
Scientific reproducibility: independent evidence supports the same scientific conclusion.

This project primarily demonstrates the first two on a small synthetic test fixture. It does not demonstrate clinical validation or independent scientific replication.






ImportantEngineering evidence has a scope



A successful Nextflow run proves that configured tasks completed. A valid BAM proves that the file passes selected structural checks. A container digest identifies image content. None of these facts alone proves that a method is appropriate for diagnosis, that a biological conclusion is correct or that the workflow is production-ready.

text:
1.17 Common misconceptions

1.17.1 “Conda and Docker do the same thing”
Both help control software, but at different boundaries. Conda manages packages inside an environment. An OCI image packages a broader userspace and metadata. We will use Conda to resolve tools and then package that environment in an image.


1.17.2 “Nextflow runs the cluster”
Nextflow models and submits work. SLURM manages shared cluster resources. The Nextflow SLURM executor connects the two.


1.17.3 “The container includes my input data”
Our image contains software, not the large analysis inputs. At runtime, files are normally mounted or staged into the container.


1.17.4 “If CI is green, the pipeline is validated”
CI reports only the checks we encoded. Validation requires defined intended use, requirements, acceptance criteria, evidence and—where applicable—formal quality or regulatory processes.


1.17.5 “GitHub is Git”
Git is the version-control system. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform built around Git repositories. Git works without GitHub.

text:
1.21 What to remember

Biological validity and engineering reproducibility support one another but are not the same claim.
A tool performs an operation; a workflow engine coordinates operations and their dependencies.
Modules, Conda, containers, Nextflow and SLURM solve different problems and can be used together.
Docker/OCI builds and distributes the image; Singularity/Apptainer executes that packaged environment on our HPC system.
Git records source history; GitHub supports collaboration; CI/CD automates explicitly defined checks and delivery.
Every green check, checksum and report has a limited meaning. Good engineers state that meaning accurately.

text:
2.1 Why a biologist should care
Graphical applications hide many implementation details. That is convenient for interactive work, but it makes a procedure difficult to record exactly. The command line turns an action into text that can be reviewed, saved in a script, placed under version control and executed by a workflow engine.
For example, “I clicked the alignment button” omits the program version, reference, input files and parameters. A command can make those choices explicit:
You do not need to understand this Bowtie2 command yet. Notice only that it is text. Later, the same text can be tested manually, saved in Bash and placed inside a Nextflow process.
The terminal is powerful because it exposes exact actions. It is risky for the same reason: the shell will attempt exactly what you request, including a badly targeted deletion. Safe command-line work begins with orientation and verification, not speed.

2.3 Terminal, shell and prompt
A terminal is the application window that displays text and sends your keystrokes. Terminal.app, iTerm2, a VS Code terminal and an SSH terminal are examples.
A shell is the program that reads and interprets commands. Common shells include Bash and Zsh. macOS commonly starts Zsh; many Linux and HPC systems use Bash.
A prompt is the text the shell displays when it is ready. It may contain a username, computer name, directory or active Conda environment.
(base) [alex@compute-1 project]$
Do not copy the prompt into a command. In this book:
pwd
means type only pwd, then press Return or Enter. The fenced block is not part of the command either.






WarningDo not copy prompt characters



Documentation sometimes shows commands beginning with $. That symbol usually represents the prompt, not text to type. Our copyable command blocks omit it. Expected output is displayed in separate text blocks.

2.5 Before you type: identify your shell and location
Run:
printf 'shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"
pwd
The first command prints your configured login shell. pwd means print working directory.
Example output on macOS:
shell=/bin/zsh
/Users/alex
Example output on Linux or an HPC system:
shell=/bin/bash
/home/alex
Your output will differ. A different username or home path is not a failure.

2.5.1 Read the first command
printf 'shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"
│      │             └─ expand the SHELL environment variable safely
│      └─ format: text, a string placeholder, then a newline
└─ print formatted text
Double quotes preserve the expanded value as one argument. We will return to quoting later.

2.7 Build a safe practice workspace
First, inspect the intended parent:
printf 'home=%s\n' "$HOME"
ls -ld "$HOME"
Then create a new, narrowly named directory:
mkdir -p "$HOME/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-02"
cd "$HOME/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-02"
pwd
mkdir creates a directory. -p also creates missing parent directories and does not fail if the directory already exists. cd changes the shell’s current directory.
Expected final line, with your home path:
/Users/alex/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-02
or:
/home/alex/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-02






ImportantThe working-directory rule



Before a command creates, moves or changes files, run pwd and inspect the target path. Most “the command ran but I cannot find the file” problems begin with an incorrect working directory.

2.9 Create predictable text files
Use printf rather than an interactive editor so the starting content is exact:
printf 'sample\tcondition\nS01\tcontrol\nS02\ttreated\n' > samples.tsv
printf 'quality-control notes\n' > notes.txt
The > operator redirects standard output into a file. It creates the file if needed and replaces its contents if it already exists.
Inspect before and after using redirection. Do not casually redirect into a valuable file.
List the result:
ls -lh
-h asks ls to show human-readable sizes when used with -l.
Expected names:
notes.txt
samples.tsv

2.10 Inspect content without editing it
Run:
cat notes.txt
head -n 3 samples.tsv
tail -n 1 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
What they do:

cat writes complete file content to standard output. Use it only for small text files.
head -n 3 writes the first three lines.
tail -n 1 writes the final line.
wc -l counts newline characters, which normally corresponds to line count for a well-formed text file.

Expected output includes:
quality-control notes
sample  condition
S01 control
S02 treated
S02 treated
3 samples.tsv
For a large log or report, use less filename to page through content without loading everything into an editor. Press q to leave less.

2.11 File extensions are names, not guarantees
samples.tsv suggests tab-separated values, but the extension does not enforce the format. The content and the consuming program determine whether the file is valid.
Likewise, renaming notes.txt to notes.fastq would not turn it into FASTQ. This is why later chapters use structural checks rather than trusting names.

text:
2.12 Copy and move safely
Create two subdirectories:
mkdir -p input archive
Copy the sample sheet:
cp samples.tsv input/samples.tsv
Move the notes:
mv notes.txt archive/notes.txt
Verify:
find . -maxdepth 2 -type f -print
Expected paths:
./archive/notes.txt
./input/samples.tsv
./samples.tsv
cp creates another file. mv changes a name or location; on the same filesystem it does not make a second independent copy.
We supplied explicit destination filenames. That makes the intended result clearer than relying on implicit directory behavior.

2.13 Standard input, output and error
A command-line process normally has three standard streams:








Stream
Number
Default destination/purpose




standard input
0
data entering the process, often the keyboard


standard output
1
expected program output, normally the terminal


standard error
2
diagnostics and errors, normally the terminal



Separating output from diagnostics lets us save a clean result while retaining an error log.
Run a successful listing and redirect standard output:
ls input > input-files.txt
Now deliberately request a missing directory and redirect standard error:
ls missing-directory 2> expected-error.txt
The second command should print nothing to the terminal because its error was redirected. Inspect it:
cat expected-error.txt
The exact wording varies, but it should say that missing-directory does not exist.
Useful forms:







Syntax
Effect




> file
replace file with standard output


>> file
append standard output to file


2> file
replace file with standard error


2>&1
send standard error to the current standard-output destination



Redirection is handled by the shell before the program starts. The program may not know that its output is going to a file.

section: 2.14 Exit status: success is a number
text:
2.14 Exit status: success is a number
When a command finishes, it returns an integer exit status. By Unix convention:

0 means success;
a nonzero value means some kind of failure or special condition.

Immediately after the deliberate failed ls, run:
printf 'exit_status=%s\n' "$?"
You should see a nonzero value such as:
exit_status=1
Now run:
ls input
printf 'exit_status=%s\n' "$?"
Expected final line:
exit_status=0
$? contains only the status of the most recently completed foreground pipeline. Even echo or printf replaces it. Capture or inspect it immediately.






WarningOutput is not the same as success



A program can write warnings and still exit zero. A program can also produce a partial output before failing. Check exit status and validate important outputs.

title: 2  The terminal, files, paths and commands
text:
2.15 Pipes connect processes
The pipe operator | connects the standard output of the command on the left to the standard input of the command on the right.
find . -maxdepth 2 -type f -print | sort
find emits paths. sort receives those paths and prints them in order.
Another example:
printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n' | wc -l
Expected output:
3
A pipe passes data; it does not automatically create an intermediate file. In Chapter 13 we will see why a failure on the left side of a pipeline can be hidden unless Bash pipefail behavior is enabled.

title: 2  The terminal, files, paths and commands
text:
2.16 Quoting prevents accidental reinterpretation
The shell performs expansions before launching a program. Spaces can divide one intended path into multiple arguments.
Create a file whose name contains a space:
printf 'temporary example\n' > "name with spaces.txt"
Read it correctly:
cat "name with spaces.txt"
Double quotes allow variable expansion while preserving the result as one argument:
practice_dir="$HOME/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-02"
printf 'practice_dir=%s\n' "$practice_dir"
Single quotes preserve literal text:
printf '%s\n' '$HOME is written literally inside single quotes'
Expected output begins with the characters $HOME; the variable is not expanded.
The safe default is to double-quote variable expansions unless you have a specific, understood reason not to.

title: 2  The terminal, files, paths and commands
text:
2.17 Wildcards expand to matching pathnames
Create three small files:
printf 'R1\n' > sample_R1.fastq
printf 'R2\n' > sample_R2.fastq
printf 'report\n' > sample_report.txt
Inspect a wildcard before using it in a command that modifies files:
printf '%s\n' sample_*.fastq
Expected matches:
sample_R1.fastq
sample_R2.fastq
The shell expands * before starting printf. Quoting the pattern changes the meaning:
printf '%s\n' 'sample_*.fastq'
This prints the literal asterisk.






ImportantInspect globs before modifying files



Never assume a wildcard matches only the intended files. Print or list the matches first. An empty or overly broad match can cause surprising behavior.

text:
2.18 Hidden files and configuration
Names beginning with . are conventionally hidden:
printf 'practice configuration\n' > .practice-config
ls
ls -la
The first listing normally omits .practice-config; the second includes it.
Git metadata lives in a hidden .git directory. Conda, Nextflow, Docker and other tools also use hidden files or directories. “Hidden” does not mean unimportant or secure.

2.19 Command history and sensitive information
Most interactive shells store command history. This helps repeat and audit work, but it creates a security risk if a command includes a password, token or private URL.
Never paste secrets directly into commands merely because a tutorial shows an environment variable. Use the authentication mechanism recommended by the service, and treat terminal transcripts as potentially sensitive.
We will never commit secrets, patient paths or credentials to the public tutorial repository.

text:
2.22 Common failures and how to reason about them

2.22.1 “No such file or directory”
First ask:
pwd
ls -la
Then inspect the parent directory and spelling. Do not immediately create a new file with the missing name; you may simply be in the wrong directory.


2.22.2 “Permission denied”
Inspect the path and permissions:
ls -ld .
ls -l samples.tsv
Do not solve every permission error with sudo or broad write permissions. On an HPC system, the correct solution may be to use project storage or ask an administrator.


2.22.3 A command appears to hang
It may be waiting for input, processing a large file or displaying through a pager. Read the screen. q exits less; Control-C requests interruption of a foreground command. Interruption may leave partial files, which must be validated before reuse.


2.22.4 A wildcard prints literally
Either it was quoted or no path matched and the shell preserved the pattern. Check the working directory and list candidate names.


2.22.5 $? unexpectedly says zero
You probably ran another successful command before inspecting it. Exit status must be captured immediately after the command of interest.

title: 2  The terminal, files, paths and commands
text:
2.25 Interview grill: ten questions
Try answering aloud before opening the model points. A strong answer explains behavior and risk; it does not merely expand an acronym.

What is the difference between a terminal and a shell?
What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
Why should a script quote a variable such as "$input_file"?
What is the difference between > and >>?
What do standard input, standard output and standard error represent?
What does exit status zero mean, and what does it not prove?
What does a pipe do, and why can pipelines complicate error detection?
Who expands *.fastq: the shell or the bioinformatics program?
How would you investigate “No such file or directory” safely?
Why is placing a password or token directly in a shell command dangerous?







NoteModel answer points






A terminal is the interface; a shell interprets commands.
An absolute path starts at root; a relative path is resolved from the current directory.
Quoting prevents whitespace and wildcard characters in the expanded value from becoming unintended argument boundaries or pathname expansions.
> replaces a file with redirected output; >> appends.
They are the process’s conventional input, expected output and diagnostic streams, numbered 0, 1 and 2.
Zero means the program reported success. It does not prove that outputs are complete, scientifically sensible or appropriate for the intended use.
A pipe connects one process’s output to another’s input. Without appropriate shell settings, the final command’s status can hide an earlier failure.
The shell normally expands an unquoted wildcard before launching the program.
Check pwd, list the directory, inspect spelling and parent paths, then determine whether the file is absent or the working directory is wrong.
Commands may be stored in history, logs, process listings or transcripts. Use purpose-built credential storage and scoped secrets instead.

text:
2.26 What to remember

Always establish the working directory and exact target before changing files.
The shell interprets quoting, variables, wildcards, pipes and redirection before or while launching programs.
Standard output and standard error can be recorded separately, and exit status must be checked immediately.
A zero exit status is necessary evidence of reported success, not sufficient evidence of a valid scientific result.
Inspect first. Use narrow paths. Avoid destructive shortcuts.

section: 3.4 The vocabulary: distribution, package manager, environment and channel
text:
3.4 The vocabulary: distribution, package manager, environment and channel
These names are easy to blur together.

Conda is a package and environment manager.
A Conda distribution is a bootstrap installation containing Conda and supporting files.
Miniforge is a small Conda distribution configured for the community-run conda-forge package channel.
Anaconda Distribution is a larger commercial distribution containing many packages and additional products.
A package is an installable unit such as samtools plus metadata.
An environment is an isolated directory containing a selected collection of packages.
A channel is a repository from which Conda obtains packages and metadata.

This book recommends Miniforge for a new personal installation because it is a small, community-focused entry point. It does not require replacing a working, institutionally managed Conda installation.
The official Miniforge project publishes installers for supported operating systems and architectures. Always recheck that page because filenames and requirements change.

title: 3  Set up and audit the learning workstation
text:
3.5 Audit before installing
Open a new terminal. Do not activate a project environment yet.

3.5.1 Identify the shell
printf 'login_shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"
printf 'current_process=%s\n' "$0"
$SHELL usually records your configured login shell. $0 describes the current shell or script. They can differ—for example, a Bash script can run from an interactive Zsh session.


3.5.2 Identify the operating system and architecture
Commands and installer files are platform-specific:
uname -s
uname -m
Common results include:



uname -s
uname -m
Meaning




Darwin
arm64
macOS on Apple silicon


Darwin
x86_64
macOS on an Intel processor


Linux
x86_64
64-bit Intel/AMD Linux


Linux
aarch64
64-bit ARM Linux



On macOS, add:
sw_vers
On Linux, inspect the distribution metadata:
cat /etc/os-release
Do not run macOS installation commands merely because they appear above Linux commands on a webpage. First match both the operating system and architecture.


3.5.3 Understand PATH
When you type a command without a slash, the shell searches directories listed in PATH, from left to right:
printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'
If two directories contain java, the first matching path wins. Conda activation and HPC modules work partly by changing this search order.
Use the shell’s own lookup command:
command -v java
command -v conda
command -v git
Possible interpretations:

a path: the shell found an executable;
an alias or function description: the name is being intercepted by the shell;
no output with a nonzero status: the shell cannot currently resolve it.

which is widely available, but command -v is a shell builtin with more predictable behavior for scripts.






WarningNot found does not mean not installed



If command -v tool prints nothing, the tool may be absent, installed outside PATH, available only after loading an HPC module, or provided only inside a container. Investigate before installing another copy.

3.6 Build a read-only inventory
Create a practice directory:
mkdir -p "$HOME/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-03"
cd "$HOME/nextflow-for-biologists-practice/chapter-03"
pwd
Start the report without including environment variables, which may contain tokens or credentials:
{
  printf '=== WORKSTATION IDENTITY ===\n'
  date
  printf 'os=%s\n' "$(uname -s)"
  printf 'architecture=%s\n' "$(uname -m)"
  printf 'login_shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"
  printf 'working_directory=%s\n' "$PWD"
} > setup-check.txt
The braces group several commands so one redirection captures their combined standard output. $(...) is command substitution: the shell runs the inner command and inserts its output.
Inspect before continuing:
cat setup-check.txt

text:
3.7 A reusable audit function
Typing the same test seven times invites inconsistency. Define a small function for the current shell:
check_command() {
  command_name="$1"

  if command -v "$command_name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf '%-12s FOUND  %s\n' \
      "$command_name" \
      "$(command -v "$command_name")"
  else
    printf '%-12s MISSING_OR_NOT_ON_PATH\n' "$command_name"
  fi
}
Use it:
{
  printf '\n=== COMMAND LOCATIONS ===\n'
  check_command git
  check_command conda
  check_command mamba
  check_command java
  check_command nextflow
  check_command docker
  check_command quarto
  check_command code
  check_command singularity
  check_command apptainer
  check_command sbatch
} >> setup-check.txt
This function reports state; it does not modify the machine.

title: 3  Set up and audit the learning workstation
text:
3.8 Tool-by-tool decisions

3.8.1 Git: required on a workstation
Git records changes to the book project and pipeline repository. Chapter 5 teaches its mental model; here we only verify the executable.
command -v git
git --version
If Git is absent:

macOS: follow the official Git installation guidance, which describes the Xcode Command Line Tools and official installer paths;
Debian/Ubuntu workstation: use the distribution package manager only if you administer the machine;
Fedora/RHEL workstation: use the documented distribution package manager;
managed HPC: ask whether Git is already installed or available as a module. Do not use sudo.

Example commands for a personally administered Linux workstation are:
# Debian or Ubuntu workstation only
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git

# Fedora workstation only
sudo dnf install git
Do not copy both branches. Choose the one matching your distribution.


3.8.2 Conda through Miniforge: required for the local Conda path
Audit both the command and its base installation:
command -v conda
conda --version
conda info --base
If those commands work, keep the installation for now. Record it. Do not stack a second Miniforge installation on top.
For a new personal macOS or Linux installation, use the installer appropriate to uname -s and uname -m from the official Miniforge releases. The interactive shell installer pattern documented by Miniforge is:
curl -L -O \
  "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"

ls -lh "Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash "Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
The installer asks where to install and whether to initialize Conda for the current shell. Read each prompt. After installation, close and reopen the terminal, then verify:
conda --version
conda info --base
On a shared HPC system, first ask whether Conda is provided and where personal environments should live. Home quotas are often too small for large package caches.






NoteMiniforge, Miniconda and Anaconda



All can provide the conda command. Seeing (base) in a prompt means a base environment is active; it does not identify the distribution reliably. Use conda info --base and institutional documentation instead of guessing.




3.8.3 Java: required to launch Nextflow
Nextflow is a Java application. Its current official installation guidance requires Java 17 or later. Verify the executable and read the first lines of its diagnostic output:
command -v java
java -version
Java traditionally writes version information to standard error, so this is normal:
java -version > java-version.txt 2>&1
head -n 3 java-version.txt
Do not assume a larger Java version number is always safer. A workflow may be validated against a supported range, and an HPC build may behave differently from a desktop build. Record the exact runtime.
On HPC, Java is commonly selected through a module:
module avail java
module load java/<site-version>
java -version
<site-version> is a placeholder. Never type angle-bracket placeholders literally. Chapter 4 explains modules and the DLDCC Java workaround from the companion project.


3.8.4 Nextflow: required, but keep the launcher separate
Verify:
command -v nextflow
nextflow -version
The launcher and workflow dependencies solve different problems. Nextflow can live in a user-controlled bin directory while FastQC and Bowtie2 live in a Conda environment or container.
For a personal Unix-like workstation, consult the official Nextflow installation page and verify Java first. A cautious form of the official bootstrap process is:
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
mkdir -p "$HOME/nextflow-download"
cd "$HOME/nextflow-download"

curl -fsSLo get-nextflow.sh https://get.nextflow.io
less get-nextflow.sh
bash get-nextflow.sh
chmod u+x nextflow
mv nextflow "$HOME/.local/bin/nextflow"
Then ensure the user bin directory is on PATH for the current session:
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
command -v nextflow
nextflow -version
Persisting the PATH change belongs in the startup file for your actual shell, such as ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc. Do not edit both blindly.
The companion project uses a repository-local launcher at ./bin/nextflow so the execution evidence refers to a known project entry point.


3.8.5 Docker: required only for building locally
docker --version verifies the client program, but not the engine:
command -v docker
docker --version
docker info
Interpret them separately:

docker --version can succeed while Docker Desktop or the daemon is stopped;
docker info must communicate with the engine;
docker run --rm hello-world additionally tests pulling and executing an image, which requires network access on the first run.

On macOS, follow Docker’s official Docker Desktop installation guide and choose the Apple-silicon or Intel download that matches uname -m. Check your organization’s Docker Desktop licensing policy before professional use.
On a personally administered Linux workstation, follow the official Docker Engine instructions for your distribution. Do not copy a package recipe for a different Linux distribution.
Docker is commonly unavailable on multi-user HPC compute nodes because its daemon and privilege model require site-level administration. This is not a defect in the cluster. We build an OCI image on an appropriate workstation or CI runner, then run it through Singularity/Apptainer in Chapter 19.






WarningThe Docker group is security-sensitive



On Linux, membership in the docker group can confer root-equivalent control of the host. Do not change groups, socket permissions or daemon configuration on a managed system. Follow local security policy.




3.8.6 Quarto: required only for writing this book
Readers following the bioinformatics workflow do not need Quarto. Authors and contributors use it to render the tutorial:
command -v quarto
quarto --version
Installers and current platform requirements are on the official Quarto download page. Treat Quarto as documentation tooling, not a biological dependency.


3.8.7 A text editor: required; an IDE is optional
Any plain-text editor is sufficient. Visual Studio Code is a convenient option because the Nextflow project provides an official extension, but the concepts do not depend on it.
If the code command is configured:
command -v code
code --version
The graphical editor may be installed even when its terminal command is not on PATH. That is another example of “not found” not proving “not installed.”
Never use a word processor that silently adds rich-text formatting to .nf, .yml, .sh or .md files.

3.12 Common failures and how to reason about them

3.12.1 command not found after installation
Open a new terminal, identify the current shell, inspect PATH, and locate the installation directory. Do not reinstall immediately.
printf 'shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"
printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'


3.12.2 The wrong architecture installer was downloaded
Stop before running it. Compare the filename with uname -m. Apple arm64 and Intel x86_64 binaries are not interchangeable assumptions.


3.12.3 java -version shows an unexpected runtime
Compare:
command -v java
type -a java
printf '%s\n' "$JAVA_HOME"
type -a can reveal several candidates. Conda activation or a module may have placed another Java earlier in PATH.


3.12.4 Nextflow says Java is missing or incompatible
Run Java independently before debugging Nextflow:
java -version
printf 'java_exit=%s\n' "$?"
Then record JAVA_HOME, JAVA_CMD and NXF_OPTS only if they are set. Do not paste an entire environment dump into a public issue because it may contain secrets.


3.12.5 docker --version works but docker info fails
The client exists but cannot reach an engine. On a workstation, start Docker Desktop or the approved Docker service. On HPC, stop: a Docker daemon may be intentionally unavailable.


3.12.6 Conda appears twice
Inspect all resolutions:
type -a conda
conda info --base
printf '%s\n' "$CONDA_PREFIX"
Multiple installations can create incompatible base libraries and confusing shell initialization. Choose deliberately rather than deleting paths at random.


3.12.7 A home directory fills during setup
Caches can be large. Inspect usage with site-approved commands and move caches only to an approved project or scratch path. Chapter 4 covers quotas and the real DLDCC failure in which Nextflow’s downloaded JAR was truncated.

text:
3.15 Interview grill: ten questions
Answer aloud before opening the model points.

What is the difference between software being installed and being on PATH?
Why do uname -s and uname -m matter before downloading an installer?
What does command -v prove, and what does it not prove?
Why keep bioinformatics tools in a project environment instead of installing them globally?
What is the difference between Conda, Miniforge, an environment and a channel?
Why can docker --version succeed while docker info fails?
Why is Docker commonly unavailable on managed HPC systems?
How can activating Conda or loading a module change which Java runs?
What evidence would you collect before reporting that Nextflow cannot find Java?
Why is an unfiltered environment dump unsafe to attach to a public bug report?







NoteModel answer points






Installed software may exist on disk while its directory is absent from the shell’s search path. PATH controls name resolution, not existence.
Installers target an operating system and processor architecture. A Darwin ARM binary is not the same artifact as Linux x86-64.
It proves how the current shell resolves a name. It does not prove that the program runs correctly, that a service is available or that the version is suitable.
Project isolation records dependencies, reduces conflicts and lets another person reconstruct the analysis without modifying the whole host.
Conda manages packages/environments; Miniforge bootstraps Conda with conda-forge defaults; an environment is an isolated package prefix; a channel is a package repository.
The client executable can print its own version without communicating with the Docker engine. docker info requires a reachable, authorized daemon.
Docker’s daemon and privilege model require host administration and can conflict with multi-user security. HPC sites commonly provide Singularity/Apptainer instead.
Both can prepend directories to PATH and may set variables such as JAVA_HOME, causing a different executable to resolve first.
Record the OS/architecture, command -v java, type -a java, java -version, command -v nextflow, nextflow -version output and only relevant Java/Nextflow variables.
Environment variables may contain tokens, credentials, private endpoints, usernames or other sensitive configuration unrelated to the failure.

4.1 Why a biologist should care
A laptop usually has one user making immediate decisions. An HPC cluster is a shared system where many users compete for finite processors, memory, storage bandwidth and accelerators. The scheduler must decide where and when work runs.
That changes the meaning of familiar actions:
AI can draft a batch script in seconds. It cannot know unwritten site policy, your allocation, your data governance requirements or the real resource profile of your sample unless you provide and verify that context.

4.2 Engineering objective

your terminal
    │ SSH

text:
4.3 The four states people accidentally collapse into one
An interview-quality explanation separates these states:

Submitted: the scheduler accepted a job description and assigned an ID.
Pending: the job is waiting for resources, priority, dependencies or a policy condition.
Running: commands are executing inside an allocation.
Completed: the scheduler received a zero process exit status.

None of those alone proves that the correct sample, reference, parameters or outputs were used. Scientific validation is a separate layer.

4.4 Before you type: identify the site and policy

What scheduler is used: SLURM, PBS, LSF or something else?
What partitions or queues may your account use?
Which project or billing account should jobs charge?
Where should large inputs, caches, temporary work and final results live?
Are login-node CPU, memory and time limits enforced?
Which container runtime is supported?
How are protected or regulated datasets governed?

text:
4.7 Compute nodes and allocations
A compute node contributes resources such as:

CPU cores or hardware threads;
RAM;
local temporary storage;
GPUs or other accelerators; and
access to shared filesystems and high-speed networking.

An allocation is permission to use a specified resource bundle for a limited time. It can be interactive or batch-oriented.
Interactive allocations are useful for small debugging sessions when the site permits them. A common SLURM pattern is:
srun \
  --partition=<partition> \
  --account=<account> \
  --cpus-per-task=2 \
  --mem=4G \
  --time=00:15:00 \
  --pty bash
Angle-bracket values are placeholders. Site documentation may require salloc followed by srun, or prohibit interactive jobs in some partitions.
Batch jobs are preferable for reproducible work because the request and command can live in a reviewed file.

4.9 Inspect the cluster without submitting work

4.9.1 Partitions and nodes with sinfo
sinfo
A compact site-specific view might be:
sinfo -o '%P|%a|%l|%D|%c|%m'
The fields request partition, availability, time limit, node count, CPUs and memory. Output formats and configured values vary by SLURM version and site.
Read the evidence as policy and capacity, not a promise that resources are immediately available.


4.9.2 Your jobs with squeue
squeue --me
If the installed SLURM version lacks --me, use:
squeue -u "$USER"
Important state codes include:

PD: pending;
R: running;
CG: completing; and
site- or version-dependent failure/hold states.

For a pending job, inspect the reason column before changing the request. A job waiting for resources is different from one held for an invalid account.


4.9.3 Historical evidence with sacct
sacct \
  --starttime today \
  --user "$USER" \
  --format=JobID,JobName,Partition,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS
Accounting fields depend on site configuration. MaxRSS may be delayed or absent. A COMPLETED state and 0:0 exit code mean the scheduled process reported success; inspect application logs and outputs next.

title: 4  HPC mental model: nodes, schedulers, software and storage
text:
4.10 Resource requests are engineering hypotheses

4.10.1 CPUs
In a typical single-program job:
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
This allocates four CPUs to one task. The application must also be configured to use four threads:
tool --threads "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"
If the tool is single-threaded, most allocated CPUs remain idle. If the tool silently starts more threads than allocated, it can oversubscribe the node.


4.10.2 Memory
These requests are not interchangeable:
#SBATCH --mem=8G
requests memory for the job allocation on a node, whereas:
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G
scales memory with allocated CPUs. Exact semantics should be checked against site policy, especially for multi-node jobs.
Requesting far too little causes out-of-memory failure. Requesting far too much can delay scheduling and waste charged capacity. Start from test data or prior accounting evidence, then revise with margin.


4.10.3 Time
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
This is a maximum wall-clock duration, not predicted CPU time. A job that exceeds it is terminated. A grossly inflated time request may make backfilling harder and delay the job.


4.10.4 Concurrency
These are different scaling dimensions:

threads: one process uses several CPUs;
processes: several programs run at once;
samples: workflow tasks may execute concurrently;
nodes: a distributed program spans computers.

Giving every task all available CPUs can reduce total throughput when many samples could have run simultaneously. Industry interviews often probe this tradeoff.

4.11 Read an AI-generated batch script critically
Consider this small template:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=inventory-test
#SBATCH --partition=<partition>
#SBATCH --account=<account>
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --time=00:05:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail

printf 'job_id=%s\n' "$SLURM_JOB_ID"
printf 'node=%s\n' "$(hostname)"
printf 'cpus=%s\n' "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"
Before submission, the human reviewer must answer:

Do the partition and account exist and permit this job?
Does logs/ exist before SLURM tries to open the output files?
Is Bash available at the resolved interpreter path?
Are two CPUs and 2 GB justified by the command?
Are all required input paths visible from compute nodes?
Will shell initialization, modules or Conda be established explicitly?
Could any printed value expose sensitive information?
What output proves that the intended program ran?

Create the log directory before submission:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch inventory-test.sh
Submission output such as Submitted batch job 123456 proves only scheduler acceptance.

text:
4.12 Environment Modules: controlled shell transformations
Clusters may install several versions of Java, compilers and applications. The module system exposes a selected version by modifying environment variables. The Lmod user guide describes this behavior.
Common inspection commands are:
module avail
module list
module show java/<site-version>
Common state changes are:
module purge
module load java/<site-version>
module load singularity/<site-version>
module purge unloads module-managed state. It does not uninstall software or delete files. module load does not copy the application into your home directory; it changes variables so the shell can find a site installation.
Many module commands print to standard error even when successful. Capture both streams when creating evidence:
module list > loaded-modules.txt 2>&1

4.12.1 Prove what a module changed
printf '%s\n' "$PATH" > path-before-module.txt
command -v java > java-before-module.txt 2>&1 || true

module load java/<site-version>

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" > path-after-module.txt
command -v java > java-after-module.txt 2>&1 || true

diff -u path-before-module.txt path-after-module.txt || true
diff -u java-before-module.txt java-after-module.txt || true
The final || true is appropriate here because diff returns 1 when files differ—the condition we are intentionally investigating.

section: 4.13 Modules and Conda are separate mechanisms
text:
4.13 Modules and Conda are separate mechanisms
This is the most important Chapter 4 distinction.
module load java/... ──► edits PATH and related variables

conda activate project ─► edits PATH and sets CONDA_PREFIX

shell resolves `java` ──► first matching executable in current PATH wins
module purge does not deactivate a Conda environment. conda deactivate does not unload a Java module. However, both operations can rearrange PATH, so the winning executable may change.
Inspect state rather than trusting the prompt:
printf 'CONDA_PREFIX=%s\n' "${CONDA_PREFIX:-NOT_ACTIVE}"
module list 2>&1
type -a java
command -v java
java -version
Order matters. If a Conda environment contains Java and is activated after the module, Conda may win. If the module prepends its Java directory later, the module may win. A pipeline should make this choice explicit.






ImportantActivation is not allocation



Loading a module or activating Conda changes the software environment in the current shell. Neither action requests CPU, memory or a compute node from SLURM.

title: 4  HPC mental model: nodes, schedulers, software and storage
text:
4.14 Singularity/Apptainer: the cluster container layer
Sites commonly provide either singularity or apptainer:
command -v singularity
singularity --version

command -v apptainer
apptainer --version
They are related HPC-oriented container runtimes, but names, versions and site configuration differ. Do not alias one name to the other without understanding the installation.
SingularityCE is designed for shared systems and normally preserves the user’s identity inside the container. Its SIF format packages a container as a single file. The official SingularityCE user guide explains its privilege and runtime model.
A container packages user-space software. It does not package the host kernel, SLURM allocation, filesystem permissions or data-governance policy. Chapter 19 develops this boundary in depth.

section: 4.15 Storage is a resource, not just a path
text:
4.15 Storage is a resource, not just a path
Typical storage classes have different purposes:








Storage
Typical use
Typical risk




Home
Small configuration, scripts, keys
Tight quota; backed up but not high-throughput


Project
Shared inputs, references, durable results
Group quota; can become globally full


Scratch
Temporary workflow work and large intermediates
Purged; not backed up


Node-local temporary
Short-lived task-local I/O
Disappears when job ends; must stage outputs back



These are common patterns, not promises. Verify your site.

4.15.1 Capacity versus quota
df reports filesystem capacity:
df -h "$HOME"
df -h /path/to/project
du estimates space used by visible files under a path:
du -sh "$HOME/.nextflow" 2>/dev/null || true
du -sh /path/to/project/work 2>/dev/null || true
quota may report a user or group limit:
quota -s
A filesystem can show hundreds of gigabytes free while your personal quota is zero. Conversely, your quota can allow growth while the shared filesystem is nearly full. Inode exhaustion can also prevent new files even when byte capacity remains.


4.15.2 Match data lifetime to storage lifetime

Keep Git-tracked code and small configuration in durable storage.
Put reusable reference data in an approved shared location.
Put Nextflow work directories and large caches where performance, quota and cleanup policy allow.
Publish final evidence out of scratch before purge deadlines.
Never use scratch as the only copy of irreplaceable data.

section: 4.16 DLDCC case study: real evidence, site-specific values
text:
4.16 DLDCC case study: real evidence, site-specific values
The companion project was validated on the DLDCC cluster at Baylor College of Medicine in August 2026. The following values are a historical snapshot, not portable defaults:
partition: main
account: waterland
container runtime: SingularityCE 4.0.3
Java module: java/jdk-18.0.1.1
The workflow later succeeded through SLURM with five separate tasks. The trace recorded native job IDs, CPU utilization, peak RSS and elapsed time.
Three failures teach more than the successful command.

4.16.1 Failure 1: Java existed but its default garbage collector crashed
The site Java executable was found, yet initialization failed inside the G1 garbage collector. The verified workaround was:
module purge
module load java/jdk-18.0.1.1
export NXF_OPTS='-XX:+UseSerialGC'
java $NXF_OPTS -version
Lesson: command -v java proves resolution, not runtime health. Test the runtime independently and record unusual JVM options.


4.16.2 Failure 2: filesystem free space did not prevent a quota error
Nextflow attempted to place its framework JAR under the default home cache and failed with Disk quota exceeded. The partially written JAR then appeared corrupt.
The fix was to place Nextflow state on approved project storage:
export NXF_HOME="$PWD/.nextflow"
Lesson: diagnose the first write failure before replacing the application. A corrupt cache file can be a downstream symptom of quota exhaustion.


4.16.3 Failure 3: the container had tools but lacked ps
The workflow tools ran in the image, but Nextflow’s task-metrics wrapper also needed ps. The first containerized run failed with:
Command 'ps' required by nextflow to collect task metrics cannot be found
Adding procps-ng to the image fixed the runtime contract.
Lesson: a process needs both scientific executables and orchestration support. An AI-generated dependency list based only on the pipeline commands may be incomplete.

title: 4  HPC mental model: nodes, schedulers, software and storage
text:
4.17 Build hpc-inventory.txt
Run this from a directory approved for small diagnostic files. It performs read-only inspection:
{
  printf '=== IDENTITY ===\n'
  date
  printf 'user=%s\n' "$USER"
  printf 'host=%s\n' "$(hostname)"
  printf 'cwd=%s\n' "$PWD"
  printf 'shell=%s\n' "$SHELL"

  printf '\n=== MODULES ===\n'
  module list 2>&1 || true

  printf '\n=== COMMAND SOURCES ===\n'
  for command_name in java conda singularity apptainer sbatch squeue sacct; do
    if command -v "$command_name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      printf '%-12s %s\n' \
        "$command_name" \
        "$(command -v "$command_name")"
    else
      printf '%-12s NOT_FOUND\n' "$command_name"
    fi
  done

  printf '\n=== ACTIVE CONDA ===\n'
  printf 'CONDA_PREFIX=%s\n' "${CONDA_PREFIX:-NOT_ACTIVE}"

  printf '\n=== SCHEDULER ===\n'
  sinfo -o '%P|%a|%l|%D|%c|%m' 2>&1 || true
  squeue -u "$USER" 2>&1 || true

  printf '\n=== STORAGE ===\n'
  df -h "$HOME" 2>&1 || true
  quota -s 2>&1 || true
} > hpc-inventory.txt
Read the syntax conceptually:

the outer braces group output into one report;
2>&1 includes diagnostic streams;
the loop applies one lookup policy consistently;
${CONDA_PREFIX:-NOT_ACTIVE} provides an explicit fallback; and
|| true allows optional site commands to be absent without truncating the inventory.

|| true is not appropriate for scientific processing steps whose failure must stop the workflow.

text:
4.22 Interview grill: ten hard questions
Answer aloud before opening the model points. These are intentionally scenario-based.

A job remains pending for two hours with reason Resources. What evidence do you inspect before requesting more resources or changing partitions?
A four-thread aligner receives --cpus-per-task=16. Describe the possible effects on utilization, queue time, throughput and accounting.
module purge was run, but the prompt still shows a Conda environment. Is that contradictory? How do you prove which Java will run?
df -h shows 700 GB free, yet Nextflow reports Disk quota exceeded and later reports a corrupt JAR. Construct the causal explanation.
A SLURM job is COMPLETED with exit code 0:0, but the BAM contains zero mapped reads. Which system succeeded, which validation failed, and what do you inspect next?
Why might requesting the maximum CPU and memory for every Nextflow process reduce total pipeline throughput?
Explain why a container can contain Bowtie2 and SAMtools yet a Nextflow task still fail because ps is missing.
An AI generates a Docker-based launch command for an HPC login node. What questions must be answered before translating it to Singularity/Apptainer?
When would you choose node-local temporary storage over shared project storage, and what correctness risk must the job handle?
Design the minimum evidence package for escalating an intermittent HPC job failure without exposing protected data or credentials.







NoteModel answer points






Inspect squeue reason and job details, partition availability, requested shape, priority/QOS/account validity and similar recent jobs. Resources means the current request cannot yet be placed; it does not automatically mean the request is too small.
The aligner may use only four CPUs while twelve sit idle. The larger shape can wait longer, reduce how many samples run concurrently and increase charged allocation without reducing runtime. Confirm whether other pipeline work shares the task before reducing it.
No. Modules and Conda are independent state mechanisms. Inspect CONDA_PREFIX, module list, type -a java, command -v java and java -version; the first matching path wins.
Filesystem capacity and user quota are different limits. The initial write was truncated when the user’s quota was exhausted; the corrupt-JAR error is a downstream symptom. Fix cache placement/quota and replace the incomplete artifact only after verifying its exact target.
SLURM successfully ran a process that reported zero. Biological/QC expectations failed. Inspect the aligner log, reference identity, read pairing, parameters, BAM header, flagstat/idxstats and input checksums.
Oversized tasks occupy scarce nodes, wait for a harder-to-place resource shape and prevent concurrent samples from using otherwise available cores. Throughput depends on the whole task graph, not one task’s maximum size.
Nextflow wraps the scientific command to stage files, capture status and collect metrics. The wrapper’s runtime dependencies are part of the container contract even when they are not biological tools.
Confirm site runtime/version, OCI compatibility, image provenance, bind paths, clean-environment behavior, user identity, GPU/MPI needs, registry access, cache placement and whether building/pulling is permitted on the cluster.
Use node-local storage for high-throughput disposable intermediates when shared I/O is a bottleneck. The job must stage inputs in and validated outputs out before termination; node-local data can disappear without recovery.
Include sanitized job ID, timestamps, state/exit code, resource request, relevant accounting metrics, module/runtime versions, container digest, command log with protected paths redacted, small non-sensitive reproducer and validation results. Exclude tokens, keys, full environment dumps and patient identifiers.

4.23 What to remember

A login node coordinates work; a scheduler allocation authorizes heavy work.
Resource requests are hypotheses to validate with measurement.
Modules and Conda are independent, but both can change executable precedence.
Filesystem capacity, quotas, inodes and retention policies are different constraints.
Scheduler success is not scientific success.
AI may draft syntax; the human remains responsible for site policy, resource reasoning, privacy and verification.

title: 19  Glossary
text:
Channel
A Nextflow dataflow object that carries values between workflow components.
Conda environment
An isolated collection of software packages and their dependencies.
Container image
An immutable package of files and metadata used to create a container runtime.
Executor
The Nextflow component that determines how tasks are launched, such as locally or through SLURM.
Process
A Nextflow definition describing a repeatable unit of work, its inputs, outputs and command script.
SLURM
A workload manager that schedules jobs and allocates shared cluster resources.
